fixes.explanation: That's the order, baker. Joseph, Jacob's son, directs the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel, and they do it (Genesis 50:2). He gives the job to the people who work for him. The next verse says the embalming takes forty days (Genesis 50:3). My oven timer would need a lie-down.

True. The verse says, “And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.” (Genesis 50:3). They mourn for Jacob, Joseph's father, and the text gives the number: seventy days. That's a long stretch on any calendar.

Yes. Joseph speaks to Pharaoh's court and asks them to pass his words to Pharaoh, Egypt's king (Genesis 50:4). In his message he says his father made him swear an oath, saying, “…‘You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.’” (Genesis 50:5). So the oath is about Canaan, and about a tomb Jacob says he dug himself.
True. Joseph says, “Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.” (Genesis 50:5). In one breath he asks to go and tells them he'll come back. Short message, clear plan.

The brothers don't stay behind, baker. The text says Joseph goes up “…along with all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household.” (Genesis 50:8). It names who stays in Goshen: only their children and flocks and herds. The brothers are on that road with him.

Yes, and nobody holds back. At the threshing floor of Atad, “…they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days.” (Genesis 50:10). That's grief out in the open. The next verse says the Canaanites living there see the mourning (Genesis 50:11).
It's the opposite, friend. The verse says they “…lamented and wailed loudly…” (Genesis 50:10). That's loud grief, not a quiet sit. Joseph mourns for his father seven days there.

Songs of praise aren't in this verse, baker. What it gives us is that they “…lamented and wailed loudly…” and that Joseph mourned for his father seven days (Genesis 50:10). That's grief out loud. I think it's good the text lets mourners be real.

The Amorites don't appear in this passage, baker. The Canaanites see the mourning at Atad and say, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). And the text says that's how the place across the Jordan came to be called Abel-mizraim. Poor Amorites didn't even get a cameo.

Flocks are a fair guess, since the passage does mention them staying in Goshen (Genesis 50:8). But the brothers' fear is about Joseph himself. They say, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” (Genesis 50:15). It's payback for what they did, and the flocks aren't part of it.
The text doesn't say Joseph gets angry, baker. It says, “When their message came to him, Joseph wept.” (Genesis 50:17). Weeping is what the verse gives us. I think this one hurts.

Soldiers is a fun guess, friend, but it's not the word they use. The brothers bow down before Joseph and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). That's the word they choose for themselves, and they say it to their own brother.

Judges isn't the word they use, baker. They bow down and say, “We are your slaves!” (Genesis 50:18). Then Joseph answers with a question: “Am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). Judges don't come up in this scene.

Leaving isn't what he says first, friend. His first words are, “Do not be afraid.” (Genesis 50:19). Later he tells them, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). Those are the words the text gives us from Joseph here.

That's the reason Joseph gives. He tells his brothers that “…God intended for good…” what they meant for evil, and he names the purpose: “…to preserve the lives of many people.” (Genesis 50:20). Joseph points to lives kept safe. That's what he says a day like this was for.

The text says Joseph does see it. “He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation…” (Genesis 50:23). Ephraim is Joseph's son (Genesis 41:52). The verse adds that the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph's knees.

A city isn't what Joseph asks for, friend. He makes them swear, “…and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” (Genesis 50:25). That's the whole request, with no city to name. I like a plain ask.
